description: We are final-year CSE students from KUET, Bangladesh, passionate about AI, machine learning, and space technology. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot data using NASA’s open datasets to improve fire monitoring and support reliable environmental analysis.
summary:
Agun Panjika (আগুন পঞ্জিকা) is an interactive, bilingual platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to address the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge.

Our application allows users to explore recent satellite-detected fire activity across 242 countries and territories through an interactive 3D Earth, maps, timelines, and downloadable reports.

NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments have different resolutions and detection sensitivities, making direct historical comparisons potentially misleading. To address this, we developed a machine-learning-assisted reconstruction system that harmonizes observations across satellite transitions. We evaluated our approach in four regions: Bangladesh, Nepal, Chin (Myanmar), and Punjab–Haryana (India), allowing users to compare reconstructed fire patterns with actual VIIRS observations.

Using NASA FIRMS and NASA POWER data, Agun Panjika combines scientific analysis with accessible visualizations, historical fire records, and English-Bangla explanations.

Our goal is to make satellite fire observations easier to understand, investigate, and interpret for students, researchers, educators, and communities while promoting environmental awareness and transparent, evidence-based analysis.
details:
Agun Panjika — A Fire History You Can Inspect

Agun Panjika is an interactive, bilingual web application that helps people explore, understand, and compare satellite-observed fire activity across the world. Developed by Team KUETaguns for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, our project addresses the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots."

The Problem

NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites have collected fire observations over many years, but their different spatial resolutions and detection sensitivities make direct historical comparisons difficult. Simply combining their detection counts can create misleading trends when the observing satellite changes. This makes it challenging to understand whether an apparent increase or decrease in fire activity reflects real changes or differences between instruments.

Our Solution

Agun Panjika combines an interactive global fire observation viewer with a machine-learning-assisted historical reconstruction system.

Users can explore a 3D Earth, select countries, visualize recent satellite detections, compare daily observations, and investigate historical fire patterns.

Our application provides:

  • Global Fire Explorer: Recent NASA MODIS and VIIRS observations covering 242 countries and territories, with interactive maps, daily charts, and satellite selection.
  • Historical Fire Reconstruction: Sensor-harmonization experiments for Bangladesh, Nepal, Chin State in Myanmar, and Punjab–Haryana in India.
  • Machine Learning: A combination of negative-binomial regression and LightGBM to reconstruct historical MODIS-era observations on a VIIRS-comparable scale, with uncertainty estimates.
  • Interactive Analysis: Users can compare original observations, correction-factor baselines, reconstructed values, and reference VIIRS observations.
  • Bangladesh Fire Almanac: Historical fire information from 2001 onward, with regional and district-level analysis, seasonal patterns, and contextual environmental information.
  • Accessible Experience: English and Bangla interfaces, interactive explanations, mobile-responsive layouts, a locally saved watchlist, offline reference information, and downloadable PNG, JSON, CSV, and PDF outputs.

Technology and Development

Our data-processing pipeline uses Python, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, statistical regression, and LightGBM. The frontend is developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, D3, and MapLibre.

The application is deployed through GitHub Pages as a Progressive Web App (PWA). Automated workflows refresh recent global satellite observations separately from the historical scientific processing.

We use NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS fire observations, NASA POWER environmental data, and additional geographic and environmental resources from ESA and other publicly available sources.

Innovation and Creativity

Our main contribution is connecting scientific satellite-data harmonization with an accessible, interactive exploration experience. Instead of presenting raw hotspot counts as directly comparable, Agun Panjika makes sensor differences, historical reconstruction, uncertainty, and reference observations inspectable.

The project combines an interactive 3D Earth, historical fire calendars, reproducible machine-learning experiments, bilingual explanations, and transparent evidence exports in a single platform.

Intended Impact

Agun Panjika aims to help students, researchers, educators, community organizations, and land managers better understand regional fire patterns and satellite observations.

The system supports environmental awareness, historical analysis, and evidence-based investigation. It is not an emergency fire-warning service, and satellite detections should not be interpreted as unique fires or exact burned areas.

Development Considerations

Throughout development, we prioritized scientific transparency, reproducibility, accessibility, accurate data attribution, responsible interpretation, mobile usability, and clear communication of uncertainty.

Our historical models were evaluated against reference observations in four regions. Further independent field validation and user testing are planned.

Ultimately, Agun Panjika aims to make complex Earth observation data more understandable, accessible, and useful to people around the world.
